findings.problem: The note says 思っている is common "for present-moment thoughts about oneself," but the example it gives (ずっとそう思っています, glossed "I've thought so all along") illustrates a continuing state, not a present-moment thought — the claim and its evidence contradict each other. For one's own opinion at the moment of speaking, plain 思う/思います is the normal choice; 思っている signals an ongoing or long-held thought (and is also the usual form for reporting someone else's thoughts).
findings.suggestion: Reword to something like: "思っている is used for a thought held over time (ずっとそう思っています, 'I've thought so all along') and for describing what someone else thinks; for your own opinion right now, 思います is normal."

findings.problem: 何を思っていますか is offered as the model for the を-object pattern, but this is not how one asks "what are you thinking?" in Japanese — that is 何を考えていますか. を思う normally carries the "think of / long for" sense (故郷を思う, 家族を思う), so the illustration points the learner at an unnatural sentence.
findings.suggestion: Replace the parenthetical with a natural を example such as 故郷を思う or 家族を思う.

findings.problem: The meaning field is a verbatim JMdict dump: fourteen glosses across three sense groups, including the redundant pair "to be realized"/"to be realised" and the colloquial interjection sense "I know!, I think so too!", which is far past what a beginner production card can cue.
findings.suggestion: Trim to a compact set such as "to understand", "to know", "to become clear", and move the colloquial "I know, right!" use to usage_notes if it is worth keeping.

findings.problem: "beach" is not a sense of うみ — the word means the body of water; a beach is 浜/砂浜/ビーチ. It reads as English-side idiom (海に行く ≈ "go to the beach") promoted to a dictionary gloss, and on the production card it invites the learner to answer うみ for the prompt "beach."
findings.suggestion: Drop "beach" from meanings, leaving "sea; ocean", and keep the beach-going idiom where it already is, in the usage note.

0c287f27aa9a.record_id: word:聖職者:せいしょくしゃ

0dab598bf6b3.record_id: word:勉強する:べんきょうする

findings.problem: The usage note says the word is almost always seen as 四つ葉のクローバー, but the example writes it in kana (よつばのクローバー), so the sentence contradicts the note and models a spelling the learner is unlikely to meet in print.
findings.suggestion: Write the example as 公園で四つ葉のクローバーを見つけました。with furigana 四[よ]つ 葉[ば], keeping the kana headword if the deck wants it.

findings.problem: The explanation that the の in 四つ葉のクローバー is the reason the word is a の-adjective states a rule that is not true — any noun takes の to modify a following noun, so this reasoning would make every noun a の-adjective; 四つ葉 is an ordinary noun here.
findings.suggestion: Drop the etymological justification and simply say that 四つ葉 is a noun used attributively with の, as in 四つ葉のクローバー.

findings.problem: The sole gloss is "Store", but both example translations render 店 as "restaurant" and "shop"; on the production card a learner prompted with "Store" alone gets no signal that 店 also covers eating places.
findings.suggestion: Add the ordinary companion glosses, e.g. "shop", "store", "restaurant (establishment)".

findings.problem: The sentence is far above a Genki-style beginner's level and its content is unhelpfully abstract: 聖職者 (clergy) and 黄金律 (Golden Rule) are both rare, low-frequency words, and 黄金律の探求をしています is stilted — 探求 normally takes an object one seeks or investigates (truth, knowledge, a cause), not a moral maxim one tries to live by, so the sentence does not clearly illustrate the listed senses.
findings.suggestion: Replace with a concrete, level-appropriate sentence using a typical collocation, e.g. 「私は真理の探求を続けています。」 ("I am continuing my pursuit of truth.") or a suru-form 「新しい音楽を探求しています。」, and prefer 探求しています over 探求をしています.

findings.problem: The note glosses 探求 as "pursuit or investigation," but "investigation/inquiry" is the sense of the homophone 探究; 探求 is seeking/searching for something, and the examples given (真理の探求, 知識の探求) are more commonly written 真理の探究 / 知識の探究 in that inquiry sense.
findings.suggestion: Limit the note to the seeking/pursuit sense and add a contrast, e.g. "Compare 探究 (たんきゅう), which is used for inquiry or research into a subject."

findings.problem: A Tokyo-dialect verb in its dictionary form is either heiban (つく + particle all high, LHH) or accented on the penultimate mora (for a two-mora verb, HLL); an odaka pattern with the fall after the verb (LHL) is not an attested accent shape for a plain-form verb, and 着く is normally cited as [1] (つ\く) only.
findings.suggestion: Keep HLL alone, or if a second attested pattern is intended, record it as the heiban LHH; drop LHL.

findings.problem: Four patterns are listed for a two-mora word but only two distinct shapes appear: LHH and HLL are each repeated. The card will draw the same diagram twice over, which reads as if もう had four accents rather than the two it has (atamadaka [1] and heiban [0]).
findings.suggestion: Deduplicate to the two distinct patterns, primary first: HLL, LHH.

findings.problem: The sentence is not a well-formed Japanese sentence: it is a verbless fragment with 貴方 dangling with no particle or predicate (「ときに貴方 祝福の導きは？」), and 「ときに」 as "by the way" is archaic/literary, so it also contradicts the "casual" register label. It reads like a clipped line of game dialogue rather than usable Japanese.
findings.suggestion: Replace with a short natural sentence in one of the listed senses, e.g. 「先生[せんせい]の導[みちび]きで、日本語[にほんご]が上手[じょうず]になりました。」 ("Thanks to my teacher's guidance, my Japanese improved.")

findings.problem: 祝福 means "blessing," not "grace," so glossing 祝福の導き as "the guidance of grace" misstates the sentence, and the usage note repeats the same wrong gloss.
findings.suggestion: If the phrase is kept, translate 祝福の導き as "the guidance of (a) blessing"; better, use the uncontroversial 神[かみ]の導[みちび]き ("divine guidance") as the illustrative phrase in the note.

findings.problem: The headword is given in bare hiragana うじ even though the card's own usage note says the place is normally written 宇治, and the example sentence follows suit (「うじに行くつもりです」). In running Japanese a place name in kana looks wrong, and bare うじ is more readily read as 氏 or 蛆 than as the Kyoto city, so the sentence does not model how the word is actually written.
findings.suggestion: Use 宇治 as the expression with reading うじ (furigana 宇治[うじ]) and write the example as 「それから、宇治に行くつもりです。」

findings.problem: The second sentence only restates the general behaviour of に/へ/で with any destination noun; it teaches nothing specific to this word, and the style guide asks for usage notes only when they teach something useful.
findings.suggestion: Keep the note about the 宇治 spelling and drop the generic particle guidance, or replace it with something word-specific (e.g. Uji's association with green tea and Byōdō-in).

findings.problem: 手 read て and glossed "hand" is a common noun, not a counter; only the suffixed ～手 (一手 いって) counts moves, and the card's own usage note says 手 "is normally a noun meaning hand." Labelling the headword a counter contradicts the note and teaches a false analysis.
findings.suggestion: Set part of speech to "noun" (mentioning the counter suffix ～手 in usage notes only).

findings.problem: Both example sentences use 手 in the "move/tactic" (board-game) sense, which is not among the card's meanings (only "Hand"), so neither example illustrates the sense the learner is being tested on.
findings.suggestion: Either add the sense to meanings (e.g. "hand", "move", "tactic") or replace one example with a sentence using 手 as a body part, e.g. 手を洗ってから食べます。

findings.problem: 「旅行にカメラをとる」 does not mean "take a camera on a trip": とる (取る) means to grasp/pick up/obtain, not to bring something along. The Japanese would be understood as picking up a camera (or misread as 撮る, "photograph a camera"), and it is exactly the false-friend use of English "take" that the card's own usage note warns against.
findings.suggestion: Replace with a sentence using a real とる sense, e.g. 「旅行の 写真[しゃしん]をたくさんとるつもりです。」 "I plan to take lots of photos on the trip." or 「そのペンをとってください。」 "Please pass/pick up that pen."

findings.problem: 「円卓へようこそ！」 does not show 円卓 in the listed sense (a physical round table) — it reads as a metaphorical welcome to a council/fantasy setting, and it sits oddly beside the usage note saying the word is formal or literary and mostly appears in set compounds like 円卓会議. As a bare exclamatory greeting it teaches neither the furniture sense nor the register the note describes.
findings.suggestion: Use a concrete sentence with the furniture sense, e.g. 「レストランの大きな円卓で家族と食事をしました。」 ("We ate with my family at the big round table in the restaurant."), or make the example one of the set phrases the note mentions, e.g. 「明日、円卓会議があります。」

findings.problem: "Colloquially 「とーちゃん」 in this text" refers to a "text" the card does not contain, so the note is unusable as written; it also spells the colloquial form with a katakana long mark instead of the usual とうちゃん/父ちゃん.
findings.suggestion: Replace with a self-contained note, e.g. "Colloquial variants: とうちゃん (父ちゃん), パパ." Better still, use the slot for the 父 vs お父さん distinction a Genki learner needs.

findings.problem: The polite (です/ます) sentence uses お父さん for the speaker's own father, which cuts against the 父 (own father, humble) vs お父さん (someone else's father, or direct address) distinction Genki teaches alongside this word — and the contrast is made sharper by 父の日 sitting in the same sentence with the ちち reading.
findings.suggestion: Either make the recipient someone else's father / a direct-address use, or add a usage note explaining that お父さん for one's own father is normal in casual family talk but 父 is used when speaking politely about him to outsiders.

findings.problem: "almost" is not a sense of すぐ; it renders the feel of もうすぐ ("any minute now"), as the card's own usage note says ("The 'almost/any minute now' feeling usually comes with もう"). Listing it as a bare meaning teaches a false gloss, and neither example sentence uses that sense.
findings.suggestion: Replace with the core senses, e.g. "immediately", "right away", "soon" (optionally "right nearby" for the distance use), and leave the もうすぐ nuance in usage_notes.

findings.problem: "A full container" is a noun gloss and misstates the na-adjective entry: as a na-adjective/adverb 一杯 means "full" or "a lot", and the container sense belongs to the counter usage the usage note itself separates out. As a result example[0] (おなかが一杯です = my stomach is full) uses a sense that no listed meaning covers.
findings.suggestion: Glosses along the lines of "full", "filled with", "a lot" — leave the "one cupful" container sense to the usage note about the counter.

findings.problem: The sentence writes the target word in hiragana (かんじ) while spelling 勉強 in kanji, which is unnatural orthography; in real Japanese this would be 漢字を勉強するつもりです。Written in kana, かんじ also reads most naturally as 感じ ('feeling'), so the sentence is ambiguous for exactly the word it is meant to illustrate.
findings.suggestion: Use 漢字を勉強するつもりです。 for the example (and consider making the headword 漢字 with reading かんじ, as the usage note itself says the word is usually written in kanji).

findings.problem: The sentence is stilted and above the stated beginner level: おかた is a dated, highly deferential word for "person" that a Genki-level learner will not meet, and the phrase reads like an old textbook set line rather than everyday speech. It also illustrates only the attributive 初めての pattern, not the core adverbial use the part of speech and gloss point at.
findings.suggestion: Use a plain adverbial example in a familiar context, e.g. 「今年、初めて日本に行きました。」"I went to Japan for the first time this year." and keep an attributive example (初めての〜) as a secondary one if the 初めての pattern is worth showing.

findings.problem: The translation "It's your first time, isn't it?" hides the structure the usage note explains — おかた is the head noun referring to the listener, so the sentence literally says "You must be a first-time visitor." The gloss and the note pull in different directions.
findings.suggestion: Translate closer to the structure, e.g. "You're here for the first time, aren't you?"

findings.problem: The meaning list is an unedited dictionary dump of ~18 senses, including entries that are meta-commentary rather than glosses ("verbalizing suffix (applies to nouns noted in this dictionary with the part of speech \"vs\")", "creates a humble verb (after a noun prefixed with \"o\" or \"go\")", "to place, or raise, person A to a post or status B"). On a beginner card this is unreadable, and it makes the production card (English -> Japanese) impossible to cue from.
findings.suggestion: Trim to the few senses the examples and usage notes actually teach — e.g. "to do", "to make (into)", "to decide on", "to cost" — and leave the suffix/humble-verb behaviour to usage_notes, which already covers the noun+する pattern.

findings.problem: The only gloss is "Chapter 1", but examples[1] uses 第１話 in the episode-of-a-series sense and translates it as "episode 1" — a sense the meanings field never lists, even though the usage note explains it.
findings.suggestion: Add "episode 1" as a second meaning alongside "Chapter 1" so both example sentences are covered by the card's glosses.

findings.problem: The card lists part of speech "noun" but also assigns verb group "suru", which suggests しごと inflects as a する-verb (しごとします). The usage note beside it correctly says the verbal form is しごとをする, so the two fields contradict each other.
findings.suggestion: Drop the verb group field for this noun (or reserve it for a separate しごとする entry) so the card does not imply a conjugation pattern the usage note denies.

findings.problem: Eight full JMdict senses, several with parentheticals ("to smell (esp. incense)", "to taste (alcohol)"), are stacked into the meaning field; for a beginner card this buries the two senses the examples actually teach and works against the compact dictionary-style gloss the deck uses.
findings.suggestion: Trim the card's meanings to the core senses ("to hear", "to listen", "to ask", perhaps "to obey, to follow (advice)") and leave the incense/alcohol and "grant a request" senses out or move them to usage_notes.

findings.problem: ありません is the polite negative, not a plain form; grouping it under "The plain negative is irregular: ない / ありません" mislabels its register.
findings.suggestion: Split by register: "The negative is irregular: plain ない, polite ありません — never あらない."

findings.problem: The gloss "to live" contradicts the card's own usage note that いる is used for people and animals; a learner could produce 母がある for "my mother lives (here)".
findings.suggestion: Drop "to live" and keep "to be, to exist, to have, to be located".

findings.problem: The example is not a sentence but a title-like noun fragment (「〜について」), and 黄金律の修復 is an unnatural collocation: 修復 is used for physically restoring damaged things (buildings, artwork, data) or for repairing relationships (関係の修復), not for reinstating an abstract moral principle. It therefore fails to show the word in either of the listed senses and contradicts the usage note printed beside it.
findings.suggestion: Replace with a concrete full sentence in one of the noted senses, e.g. 「この お寺 は 去年 修復 されました。」 ("This temple was restored last year.") or 「バックアップ から データ を 修復 しました。」

findings.problem: The example is labelled "polite", but the fragment contains no predicate at all, so it is neither polite nor plain; the label cannot be justified as written.
findings.suggestion: Give the example a 〜ます/です predicate if it is to be labelled polite, or drop the register label.

findings.problem: The sentence demonstrates 新来 with humble keigo (お伝えしたい, お〜する) plus explanatory のです, and reads as a context-dependent fragment; that is two grammar points above a Genki-style beginner's level competing with the target word.
findings.suggestion: Use a simpler, self-contained polite sentence, e.g. 新来のかたに会社を案内しました。("I showed the newcomer around the company.")

findings.problem: The sentence labeled "polite" pairs the rough pronoun お前 with 〜ですか, a register clash that is unnatural in ordinary speech; the neutral English translation gives no hint of the confrontational tone that would be needed to license it, so the card models お前は…ですか as a normal polite pattern — exactly the mistake a learner of this word is most likely to make. The usage note itself calls the combination unusual, contradicting its presentation as the card's polite example.
findings.suggestion: Replace with a plain-form sentence (e.g. お前は夏休みに京都へ行くつもりか。) or, if a polite-form example is wanted at all, use a different pronoun/omit the subject and keep お前 to the casual example.

6089834d6ff5.record_id: word:そう言えば:そういえば

findings.problem: The pattern HLLHLL has six marks, but the reading そういえば has only five morae (そ/う/い/え/ば), and it encodes two separate rises inside a single diagram. For this phrase the expected shape is そう (H-L) followed by 言えば with its accent on い (い\えば), i.e. HL-HLL over five morae, not HLLHLL.
findings.suggestion: Re-check the pattern against the reading; if そう and 言えば are treated as two accent phrases, draw them as the two accents the format supports rather than one six-mark string.

findings.problem: Four patterns are listed but only two are distinct (LHH, HLL, HLL, LHH), so the card would draw the same two diagrams twice; duplicates teach nothing and suggest a data-merge error rather than four accepted accents.
findings.suggestion: Deduplicate to the two distinct patterns, primary first (HLL, LHH — or LHH, HLL if heiban is primary for this sense).

findings.problem: 明日 read あした is a jukujikun: the reading is assigned to the compound as a whole and cannot be split as 明=あ + 日=した. The split furigana teaches two nonexistent kanji readings (the example sentence correctly uses the whole-word form 明日[あした]).
findings.suggestion: 明日[あした]

findings.problem: 明日 is a temporal noun that also functions adverbially; labelling it simply "adverb" conflicts with the card's own usage note example 明日は忙しいです, where it is the topic noun.
findings.suggestion: "noun (temporal); used adverbially" or similar.

findings.problem: The clause "It can be marked with は or を-less topic は for contrast" is garbled and does not state a usable rule.
findings.suggestion: "It can take は for contrast: 明日は忙しいです."

findings.problem: The sentence is lifted from a fantasy-game context (二本指様 "the Two Fingers") and uses 祈祷, a low-frequency compound well above a Genki-level learner; it is also an elliptical fragment rather than a full sentence, so it demonstrates 〜に興味がある only by implication.
findings.suggestion: Use a concrete everyday sentence in the same sense, e.g. 「日本の音楽に興味があります。」 ("I'm interested in Japanese music."), and keep the fragment 「ご興味は？」 as a usage note if the polite ellipsis is worth teaching.

findings.problem: The sentence is labelled "casual" but ends in the polite 〜ます set phrase よろしくお願いします, and the usage note beside it says to avoid うす in polite situations, so the card appears to contradict itself. (The mix is real in sports-club speech, but a beginner has no way to see that from the card.)
findings.suggestion: Either use an all-plain sentence (e.g. うす、今日もよろしく。) or add a short note that うす plus お願いします is the standard club/team greeting despite the polite form.

findings.problem: The headword and the example sentence spell the place name in hiragana (うじ) even though the usage note states it is normally written 宇治; bare うじ is far more likely to be read as 蛆 "maggot", and a recognition card fronted with うじ trains the wrong association (the Shirabe/jpdb lookups for うじ will also return the maggot entry).
findings.suggestion: Use 宇治 as the expression with reading うじ (furigana 宇治[うじ]) and write the sentence as それから、宇治[うじ]に行[い]くつもりです。

findings.problem: あなた is not a polite or formal way to address someone; dictionaries restrict it to addressees of equal or lower status, and using it toward a superior is rude. Glossing it "you (polite/formal)" invites exactly the mistake learners must avoid, and the usage note does not correct it (it only describes the kanji spelling's literary register).
findings.suggestion: Gloss as "you" (optionally "you (to an equal or subordinate)") and move the register facts to usage_notes, e.g. noting that あなた is not honorific and should not be used to superiors — a name plus さん or a title is used instead.

findings.problem: 貴方の見解を伺いたく is a truncated business-email fragment: it uses the humble 伺う, the noun 見解, and the elliptical 〜たく continuative that trails off mid-sentence. For a Genki-level learner this teaches an advanced ellipsis pattern rather than the word あなた, and the card itself has to explain the fragment.
findings.suggestion: Use a complete, level-appropriate sentence such as 「貴方のお名前を教えてください。」 or, if the formal written flavour of the kanji spelling matters, at least a finished sentence like 「貴方のご意見を伺いたいです。」

findings.problem: “beach” is not a sense of うみ (that is 浜/海岸/ビーチ); it only arises idiomatically in phrases like うみに行く, so listing it as a bare dictionary gloss risks the production card teaching うみ as the word for “beach.”
findings.suggestion: Keep meanings as “sea; ocean” and leave the seaside/beach nuance to the usage note, which already states it correctly.

findings.problem: する in its core sense (仕事をする, 勉強をする) takes a を object and is a transitive verb; dictionaries tag it vt. Labelling it intransitive contradicts the card's own example 仕事をします and the usage note about 何をする taking を.
findings.suggestion: Set transitivity to transitive (or omit it, since する's irregular/auxiliary uses do not reduce to a single label).

findings.problem: Eighteen senses, including metalinguistic ones ('verbalizing suffix', 'to place, or raise, person A to a post or status B'), are dumped into the meaning field; on a production card (English -> Japanese) this is unreadable and far past the beginner level the rest of the card targets.
findings.suggestion: Keep a handful of compact glosses ('to do', 'to make (into)', 'to cost', 'verb-forming suffix with nouns') and move the rest to usage_notes or leave them out.

findings.problem: The phrase "It can be marked with は or を-less topic は for contrast" is garbled — it repeats は and refers to a "を-less topic は" that means nothing to a beginner.
findings.suggestion: Simplify to something like: "It can take は for contrast or topic: 明日は忙しいです ('Tomorrow I'm busy')."

findings.problem: The Japanese is not a sentence but a truncated business-letter clause (連用中止 〜たく, expecting 〜たく存じます/お願いします), while the English translation is a complete sentence; it is also well above a Genki-level learner's grammar, and 貴方 is normally written あなた or omitted.
findings.suggestion: Use a complete, level-appropriate polite sentence, e.g. 「先生のご見解を伺いたいです。」 or 「この問題について、部長の見解を伺いました。」

findings.problem: The note reads "Colloquially 「ほーら」 in this text" — it refers to "this text", which has no antecedent anywhere on the card, and as written it tells the learner nothing usable about when the lengthened form appears.
findings.suggestion: Either drop the note or restate it as a fact about the word, e.g. "Often lengthened to 「ほーら」 for emphasis when drawing someone's attention."

findings.problem: The gloss list is a raw dictionary dump of nine senses (including "to cognize, to cognise" and "to concern", the latter only occurring in fixed negative idioms like 知ったことではない), which is far more than a beginner card can use and buries the core sense.
findings.suggestion: Trim to the senses the examples actually show, e.g. "to know", "to be aware of", "to get to know, to find out", and move the idiomatic "to concern" sense to usage_notes or drop it.

77af723df6e8.accepted_because: jpdb's API returns HLL for なる and the deck owner confirmed it against jpdb; jpdb is this deck's authority for accents. The heiban reading is the dictionary's, not the one this deck follows.

784f709e77bc.record_id: word:うんどうする:うんどうする

findings.problem: 今日 is primarily a temporal noun that also functions adverbially (今日は月曜日です, 今日の予定), so labelling it simply "adverb" understates its use — and the card's own usage note describes it as "a time word that works adverbially".
findings.suggestion: Label it as a noun (temporal noun) used adverbially, e.g. "noun, adverb".

85295c402c19.record_id: word:そう言えば:そういえば

findings.problem: The note reads "Colloquially 「そういや」 in this text." — the trailing "in this text" appears to be leftover boilerplate from a source and makes the sentence incoherent on a standalone vocabulary card; neither example contains そういや.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite as a self-contained note, e.g. "Often contracted to そういや in casual speech."

findings.problem: The claim "For present-moment thoughts about oneself, 思っている is also common" is illustrated with ずっとそう思っています ("I've thought so all along"), which is a long-held state rather than a present-moment thought, so the example contradicts the rule it is meant to support. It also omits the more useful contrast a beginner needs: for one's own current opinion the plain 思う/思います is normal, while 思っている marks an ongoing or held opinion and is required when reporting someone else's thoughts (彼は高いと思っている).
findings.suggestion: Rephrase along the lines of: "思っている expresses an opinion held over time (ずっとそう思っています, 'I've thought so all along') and is also used when reporting what someone else thinks (彼は高いと思っている); for your own opinion at the moment of speaking, plain 思う/思います is normal."

findings.problem: The first sentence is muddled about which part stays plain: it says the opinion comes first in plain form "followed by と思います, even when the rest of the sentence is polite" — but と思います *is* the polite part, and the point is that the embedded clause stays plain regardless.
findings.suggestion: "The opinion clause before と stays in plain (short) form even when the sentence ends politely in と思います."

findings.problem: Seven sense groups and roughly twenty glosses (including marginal ones like "to expect, to look forward to" and "to recall, to remember") overload a beginner card whose examples only illustrate the "to think/believe" opinion sense; the style guide asks for compact dictionary-style meanings.
findings.suggestion: Trim to something like "to think", "to believe", "to feel", and move the rarer senses to usage_notes or leave them out.

findings.problem: The example is labeled "polite" and pairs うす with 〜ます/よろしくお願いします, which contradicts the card's own usage note that うす is very casual, can sound rough, and should be avoided in polite situations; as presented it teaches that うす has a polite register.
findings.suggestion: Relabel this example as casual/in-group (e.g. a sports-club greeting to teammates) or replace it with a plain-form sentence, e.g. 「うす、おつかれ。」, and reserve the polite label for sentences that do not open with うす.

findings.problem: The example writes the word in hiragana (かんじを勉強するつもりです), which contradicts the card's own usage note that it is "usually written 漢字"; 漢字 is essentially never written in kana in real Japanese, so the sentence looks orthographically unnatural.
findings.suggestion: Write the example with the standard form and furigana: 漢字[かんじ]を 勉強[べんきょう]するつもりです。 while keeping the headword in kana if the deck wants a kana-first entry.

findings.problem: The only listed meaning is "Yotsuba (name)", but the example sentence uses よつば in its ordinary lexical sense "four-leaf" (四つ葉のクローバー = four-leaf clover), a sense the card never glosses. As written the card teaches that よつば means a girl's given name and then shows a sentence where it does not.
findings.suggestion: Add the primary sense first, e.g. meanings: "four leaves", "four-leaf (clover)", keeping "Yotsuba (given name)" as a secondary gloss; the の-adjective part of speech and the usage note then match the example.

findings.problem: The usage note says the word is "almost always seen in 四つ葉のクローバー", i.e. normally written with kanji, yet the headword and the example sentence are kana-only, so the learner never meets the form they will actually encounter.
findings.suggestion: Use 四つ葉 as the expression with reading よつば and furigana 四[よ]つ 葉[ば], and write the example as 公園で四つ葉のクローバーを見つけました。

findings.problem: よう is labeled an auxiliary verb, but the word this card actually teaches (glossed "hey; yo", used sentence-initially as a greeting) is an interjection; the card's own usage note says so explicitly, so the POS field contradicts the rest of the card and teaches a false analysis. The auxiliary よう is a separate item (volitional/conjectural suffix, as in 食べよう), not this greeting.
findings.suggestion: Set part of speech to "interjection" (or "interjection (greeting)").

findings.problem: The sentence is labeled polite and uses ですね, but pairs it with an interjection the card describes as very casual and potentially rough/masculine; the register label sits awkwardly against the usage note's "best used with close friends".
findings.suggestion: Either relabel this example as semi-casual/familiar (e.g. speaking to a close coworker) or recast it in plain form, e.g. よう、今日は早いね。

findings.problem: 花火祭り is offered as a common compound, but the standard everyday word for a fireworks event is 花火大会; 花火祭り occurs mainly inside specific event names, so it is a misleading model for a beginner.
findings.suggestion: Replace it with a genuinely common compound such as 夏祭り and 秋祭り (or 村祭り), and if fireworks are worth mentioning, point out 花火大会 instead.

findings.problem: The gloss list runs to eleven senses, most of which (to engulf, to overwhelm, to keep down/suppress, to accept a demand, to make light of, to conceal, to smoke tobacco) belong to the 呑む register and are far outside a Genki-level learner's needs; on a production card these compete with the core sense as prompts.
findings.suggestion: Trim the card to the senses the examples teach — "to drink", "to take (medicine)" — and leave the extended 呑む senses out or mention them briefly in usage_notes.

findings.problem: The meaning field is a full JMdict dump of three sense groups (15 glosses), including the interjectional "I know!, I think so too!" use, which neither example illustrates and which a beginner is likely to misread as a core meaning of the verb.
findings.suggestion: Trim to compact core glosses (e.g. "to understand", "to know", "to become clear") and move the interjection use to usage_notes if it is worth keeping at this level.

findings.problem: The example sentences write the verb in kana (しにます / しぬ) while the usage note writes it as 死ぬ; in normal Japanese text this verb is written with the kanji, so the sentences model non-standard orthography and disagree with the note beside them.
findings.suggestion: Write the sentences as 「この魚は、水がないと死にます。」 and 「このゲーム、何回も死ぬの？」 with furigana 死[し]にます / 死[し]ぬ, or drop the kanji from the usage note so the card is internally consistent.

findings.problem: The card labels あんまり a na-adjective, but every meaning listed ("not very; not much; too much; excessively") and both example sentences are adverbial; the usage note itself says it is "usually used adverbially, not as a な-adjective," so the POS field contradicts the rest of the card and could lead a beginner to produce forms like あんまりな.
findings.suggestion: Set part of speech to "adverb" (optionally noting na-adjective as a secondary, rarer use as in あんまりな話).

findings.problem: The sentence is labelled "casual" but is written in polite form (…行くつもりですか), which both mismatches the stated register and contradicts the card's own usage note that お前 with polite grammar sounds deliberately confrontational rather than neutral — so as presented it models exactly the combination the note warns against.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite in plain form to match the label and the note, e.g. お前は夏休みに京都へ行くつもりなのか。 / お前、夏休みに京都へ行くつもり？ (same English translation).

a7c022ee9846.record_id: word:勉強する:べんきょうする

findings.problem: 花火祭り is given as a common compound, but the ordinary Japanese word for a fireworks event is 花火大会; 花火祭り appears only in a few specific event names and is not a standard compound a beginner should learn alongside 夏祭り.
findings.suggestion: Replace 花火祭り with a genuinely common compound, e.g. 秋祭り (autumn festival) or 祭り日, or mention 花火大会 separately as the usual word for a fireworks display.

findings.problem: 凄い is an i-adjective (both examples use it as a predicate adjective: 凄いですね / 凄いね), but the card labels it an adverb; a learner would try to attach it directly to verbs or expect it not to conjugate.
findings.suggestion: Set part of speech to i-adjective (い-adjective). If the colloquial adverbial use (すごい美味しい) is worth teaching, put it in usage_notes rather than the POS field.

findings.problem: "Colloquially 「すげえ」 in this text." is garbled — "in this text" refers to nothing on the card, so the note states no usable rule.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite as something like "In casual (often male) speech, frequently pronounced すげえ."

findings.problem: "wow" is an interjection gloss, not a meaning of the adjective 凄い, and neither example uses it that way; it also omits the common negative sense (terrible, dreadful).
findings.suggestion: Use compact adjective glosses, e.g. "amazing", "incredible", "terrible".

findings.problem: The sentence is a fragmentary, archaic/theatrical line (no predicate, no particle after 貴方, 貴方 written in kanji) that is neither natural modern Japanese nor 'casual' register, and it is well above a Genki-level learner's grammar; it also fails to show 祝福 in the listed sense clearly ('the blessing's guidance' is opaque). The usage note itself concedes the sentence is 古風で芝居がかった, which contradicts the 'casual' label.
findings.suggestion: Replace with a short, natural sentence in one of the forms the usage note recommends, e.g. 「友[とも]だちの結婚[けっこん]を祝福[しゅくふく]した。」(I blessed / congratulated my friend on his marriage.) or 「二人[ふたり]は祝福[しゅくふく]を受[う]けました。」and drop or rewrite the note about archaic phrasing.

findings.problem: "almost" is not a meaning of すぐ — the card's own usage notes attribute that feeling to もうすぐ, not to すぐ alone, and the core sense ("immediately / right away") is absent from the gloss list while both example sentences use exactly that sense.
findings.suggestion: Gloss as "soon", "immediately", "right away" (and optionally "right nearby" for the spatial use); drop "almost".

findings.problem: The note says お姉ちゃん "may be lengthened and written おねーちゃん", but おねーちゃん is simply an alternative (casual/manga-style) orthography for the same ねえ long vowel — no extra length is implied. Actual lengthening would be written おねえちゃーん / おねーちゃーん.
findings.suggestion: Reword to something like: "In casual writing the ねえ is often spelled with a long-vowel mark: おねーちゃん."

findings.problem: The sentence is labelled casual but ends in the polite copula ですね, which clashes both with the stated register and with よう's rough, intimate-friends-only tone described in the usage notes.
findings.suggestion: Use a plain-form sentence, e.g. よう、今日は早いね。("Hey, you're early today.")

bcfb6daa9373.accepted_because: Verified against jpdb's API earlier and confirmed by the deck owner: jpdb returns HLL for なる (な high, る low), and jpdb is the accepted authority for this deck's accents. The reviewer's heiban reading is the dictionary's, not the one this deck follows.

findings.problem: なる (成る) is accentless (平板型, accent 0): な↗る stays high through a following particle. "HLL" draws it as 頭高 with a drop after な, which teaches the wrong accent and mispronounces every derived form (になります, 大きくなる).
findings.suggestion: Use the heiban pattern — LHH (low な, high る, particle slot high, no drop).

findings.problem: The meanings field is a full JMdict sense dump (eleven sense groups, ~30 glosses) rather than the compact dictionary-style list the deck calls for; on the production card a beginner is asked to produce なる from cues like "to be promoted" or "to play (the part of)", which do not match the two example sentences.
findings.suggestion: Trim to the senses the card actually teaches, e.g. "to become", "to turn into", "to get (to be)", and move the rarer senses to usage_notes or drop them.

findings.problem: The usage note states that in this sense the word is usually written 住む, but both example sentences render it in kana (すむつもりです / すんでるの), which is the less natural orthography the note itself warns against.
findings.suggestion: Write the examples with the kanji the note recommends — 来年、京都に住むつもりです。 / 今、だれと住んでるの？ — keeping the kana headword if that is the deck's convention.

findings.problem: The note is tagged part of speech "noun" yet carries a verb group of "suru"; a plain noun has no verb group, and the label invites the learner to treat しごと itself as a conjugable verb (the card's own usage note correctly says the verb is しごとをする).
findings.suggestion: Drop the verb group for this noun, or reclassify it explicitly as a suru-compatible noun (e.g. part of speech "noun (suru-verb)") so the two fields agree.

findings.problem: The meaning list is a raw JMdict dump for a beginner card: five bundled sense groups, several of which ("to come to be, to become, to get, to grow, to continue", "to come from, to be caused by") are not illustrated by either example, and the last entry "to come to (i.e. \"when it comes to spinach ...\")" is a dictionary meta-gloss rather than an English meaning, which will read as noise on the production card.
findings.suggestion: Trim to compact senses actually taught here, e.g. "to come", "to arrive", and move the auxiliary 〜てくる sense (already explained in usage_notes) out of the meanings field.

findings.problem: The note writes the collocation in mixed script (しゃしんを撮る) on a card whose headword is deliberately kana-only, so the learner is shown a kanji (撮) the card does not teach or gloss right where it is meant to learn the kana form.
findings.suggestion: Write the collocation consistently with the card, e.g. "しゃしんをとる (写真を撮る) means 'to take a photograph.'"

findings.problem: "to draw, to paint" belongs to the かく written 描く/画く, not to 書く; the card's own usage note says the drawing sense is normally spelled 描く, so the meaning list contradicts the note and would prompt 書く as the answer for "to draw" on the production card.
findings.suggestion: Limit the meanings to "to write", "to compose", "to pen" and leave the 描く/かな discussion in usage_notes.

d42bc00b5e73.record_id: word:うんどうする:うんどうする

findings.problem: The card labels 一杯 an adverb, but both example sentences use it predicatively (おなかが一杯です, 星が一杯だよ), i.e. as a な-adjective/noun rather than adverbially; a learner following the label might produce something like *一杯だ食べる or expect 一杯 to modify a verb here.
findings.suggestion: Label it as な-adjective/noun (adv only as a secondary sense), or add an adverbial example such as お腹一杯食べました so the stated part of speech matches what the sentences show.

findings.problem: 花火祭り is given as a common compound, but the standard Japanese term for a fireworks event is 花火大会; 花火祭り is at best marginal and could lead a learner to produce an odd phrase.
findings.suggestion: Replace 花火祭り with a genuinely common compound such as 秋祭り or 神社の祭り, and mention 花火大会 separately if the fireworks context is wanted.

findings.problem: The example is a mined mid-sentence fragment (ending in 〜ておりまして, with no main clause) that is far above a Genki-level learner: it pairs humble 〜ております with the rare, near-obsolete noun 示教, so the learner meets two harder unknowns than the target word, and 祈祷の示教をする is itself an odd collocation. The English translation is also a complete sentence, hiding that the Japanese is unfinished.
findings.suggestion: Replace with a short complete sentence using 祈祷 in its listed sense, e.g. 「お寺で祈祷をしてもらいました。」 ("I had a prayer ritual performed for me at the temple.")

findings.problem: The card labels ジャンボ a な-adjective while its own meaning ("Jumbo (name)") and usage note state it is a proper noun; a learner drilling this note would learn a false part of speech and expect adjectival forms like ジャンボだった/ジャンボで that do not exist for a name.
findings.suggestion: Set part of speech to noun (proper noun), and keep the usage note explaining that な in ジャンボなの？ is the copula before explanatory の.

findings.problem: ジャンボ has three morae (ジャ・ン・ボ), so with the trailing particle slot the diagram needs four positions, but HHLLL specifies five — the drawn accent cannot correspond to this reading.
findings.suggestion: Re-derive the pattern for a three-mora reading (e.g. HLL plus particle slot for an atamadaka-style reading) or drop the field rather than draw an unaligned diagram.

ee007af0037c.record_id: word:お姉ちゃん:おねえちゃん

findings.problem: The note "Colloquially 「おねーちゃん」 in this text" is incoherent: no text on the card uses that spelling, and the phrase "in this text" refers to nothing, so the learner cannot tell what is being taught.
findings.suggestion: Say what is actually useful, e.g. "Familiar/affectionate term for one's own or someone else's older sister; also used as a form of address. Casual writing sometimes spells it おねーちゃん."

findings.problem: The gloss list is a full dictionary dump for a beginner card: ten senses, several of which ("to become intimate, to take up (with somebody)", "to become pregnant", "to grow, to be raised") are rare or euphemistic and are not the senses either example or the usage notes teach, which makes the production card's target answer unclear.
findings.suggestion: Trim to the senses the card actually teaches — e.g. "to be able to do", "to be finished, to be ready", "to be made, to be built" — and leave the marginal senses to a dictionary lookup.

findings.problem: The sentence 「あさはやくおきないつもりです。」 demonstrates the word only in the negative and hangs it on 〜ないつもり, an intention-to-refrain construction that is both later-course grammar and an odd fit for waking up; the card's own usage note (time marked with に, as in 七時におきる) is not illustrated at all.
findings.suggestion: Use a plain affirmative example that shows the core sense and the に time marking, e.g. 「まいあさ ろくじに おきます。」 ("I get up at six every morning.")

findings.problem: ありません is a polite form but is listed as one of the "plain negative" forms, which could lead a beginner to use it in plain-form contexts.
findings.suggestion: Split the registers, e.g. "The negative is irregular: plain ない, polite ありません — never あらない."

findings.problem: The note ends with "in this text", a dangling reference to a source text the learner cannot see; on the card it reads as if そりゃ were somehow limited to a specific passage rather than being the general colloquial contraction of それは.
findings.suggestion: Rephrase without the source reference, e.g. "Often contracted to 「そりゃ」 in casual speech."

fd2838026f94.record_id: word:聖職者:せいしょくしゃ

findings.problem: The sentence uses 聖職者 correctly but its content is abstract and off-level for the intended learner: 黄金律 and 探求 are both low-frequency, and 〜の探求をしています reads like translationese (探求しています, or plainer 〜について考えています, would be more natural). It teaches the 〜として construction and two hard nouns rather than illuminating 聖職者 itself.
findings.suggestion: Replace with something concrete and simpler, e.g. 「父は聖職者として教会で働いています。」("My father works at a church as a member of the clergy.")

findings.problem: The example is a subordinate fragment with no main clause (「…差し支えなければ」 trailing off), so it never shows what the request or question actually is; the English gloss trails off too. A learner cannot see the noun 差し支え functioning in a complete sentence, and the fragment is labelled "polite" while containing no polite predicate at all (the politeness would live in the missing main clause).
findings.suggestion: Complete the sentence so the register is visible and the idiom's function is clear, e.g. 「差し支えなければ、お名前を教えていただけますか。」 ("If you don't mind, could you tell me your name?")
